_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- Florida rule seed, 2026-08-23. Loaded through add_rule.
Every rule below was read VERBATIM from The Florida Bar's own official rule
books before being encoded: Rules of Civil Procedure (April 1, 2026 edition),
Rules of Appellate Procedure (July 1, 2026), and Rules of General Practice and
Judicial Administration (July 1, 2026).
COMPUTATION STANDARD: fl_rgpja_2514, which is NOT a reuse of any existing
standard. Florida shifts the START of a count to the next business day and
counts that day as day one (2.514(a)(1)(A)), where the FRCP family merely
excludes the trigger day. The earlier scoping note that called Florida
'data-only, no engine change' was wrong; see the standard's own comment.
SERVICE EXTENSION: fl_rgpja_2514b adds FIVE days for service by mail only --
not the FRCP's three, and narrower in what qualifies.
EFFECTIVE_FROM IS THE EDITION DATE READ, NOT THE RULE'S OWN AMENDMENT DATE.
Illinois's rules carry a per-rule amendment history in the rule itself, so its
effective_from values trace to the real amendment that set each period. The
Florida rule books do not print that history per rule, so every row here uses
the publication date of the edition actually read: 2026-04-01 for the Rules of
Civil Procedure, 2026-07-01 for the Rules of Appellate Procedure.
CONSEQUENCE, deliberate and not a defect: a Florida matter triggered BEFORE
those dates is REFUSED rather than computed. These periods are long-standing
and almost certainly applied earlier, but 'almost certainly' is exactly what
this engine refuses to compute from -- the same call already made for
Pennsylvania, where pre-2024 matters are refused because Pa.R.C.P. 106 was
rescinded and its predecessor text was never read verbatim. To extend Florida
backwards, read the earlier edition and add a superseding row with the older
effective_from; never widen this one by assumption.
THE 45-DAY DEFENDANT CARVE-OUT, encoded as separate rows rather than folded in:
1.340(a)(9) and 1.350(b)(3) each give a DEFENDANT a longer period measured from
a DIFFERENT event -- 45 days after service of the process and initial pleading,
rather than 30 days after service of the discovery request. Two different clocks
from two different starting events cannot be one rule row, and which applies is
a case fact (is this party a defendant, and is the request early enough in the
case for the carve-out to bite). Same treatment as Michigan's in-state versus
out-of-state service rows.
NOT ENCODED, deliberately, and flagged rather than dropped:
RULE 1.442(f)(1) DISAPPLIES THE SERVICE EXTENSION OUTRIGHT -- recorded
2026-08-27 by the platform-wide extension re-read, BEFORE any row needs it.
Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.442(f)(1), on proposals for settlement, says in terms:
"A proposal is deemed rejected unless accepted by delivery of a written notice
of acceptance within 30 days after service of the proposal. THE PROVISIONS OF
FLORIDA RULE OF GENERAL PRACTICE AND JUDICIAL ADMINISTRATION 2.514(b) DO NOT
APPLY TO THIS SUBDIVISION."
NO 1.442 ROW IS SEEDED, so nothing here is wrong today. This is
disclosed-but-unreachable, the same posture as North Carolina's Rule 6(f) and
Virginia's Parts Five / Five A carve-out. It is written down so a session
seeding the 30-day acceptance period INHERITS the warning instead of
rediscovering it: that row must carry NO service_extension. Attaching the
ordinary five days would report a date FIVE DAYS LATE on a deadline whose
default outcome is that the proposal is deemed REJECTED.
Note 1.442(f)(2) as well, a different shape and also not seeded: where the
existence of a class is alleged, the acceptance time is extended to 30 days
after the certification order is FILED -- a different trigger, not a longer
period.
1. The chief-justice extension limb of 2.514 -- (a)(1)(C), (a)(3)(C) and
(a)(6)(B). Florida's hurricane mechanism: the chief justice may extend time
by order and a day inside that extension is treated like a holiday. It is
unknowable in advance. A Florida date from this engine is correct only
absent such an order, and during hurricane season that is a real caveat.
Same treatment as Indiana's office-closed limb and Illinois's
Governor-proclamation limb.
2. 2.514(a)(6)(B)'s companion limb, 'any day observed as a holiday by the
clerk's office' -- the engine has no office-closed concept, by design.
3. 2.514(a)(3), periods stated in HOURS. The engine counts days; an hour-based
period would need a different unit and its own last-day rule (2.514(a)(4)
sets 11:59:59 p.m. eastern for electronic filing). No Florida rule encoded
here is hour-based, so nothing silently falls through to day counting.
4. 1.140(a)(2)'s 40-day and 30-day periods for the State of Florida, its
agencies and officers. Real and citable, but whether a party is the state
sued in an official capacity -- and whether suit is under section 768.28 --
are case facts the engine has no field for, and guessing between three
overlapping periods is exactly what it must not do.
5. 1.140(a)(3)'s motion-tolling provision: serving a motion under the rule
ALTERS these periods. A matter with a pending Rule 1.140 motion must not
rely on the plain answer date without accounting for it.
6. 9.110(b)'s cross-reference to rule 9.140(c)(2) -- a criminal-appeal
exception outside this domain.

rules.label: Answer to a complaint after service of original process (Florida)

authority.quote: Unless a different time is prescribed in a statute of Florida, a defendant must serve an answer within 20 days after service of original process and the initial pleading on the defendant, or not later than the date fixed in a notice by publication.
authority.note: TWENTY days, not the federal 21 and not Illinois's 30 -- Florida is the shortest answer period in this engine, which makes an inherited number especially dangerous here. The rule opens with 'Unless a different time is prescribed in a statute of Florida', so a statutory override displaces this row entirely; the engine cannot see such a statute and does not look for one. NOT encoded from this same subdivision: the 40-day and 30-day periods in 1.140(a)(2) for the state, its agencies and officers, and the motion-tolling provision in 1.140(a)(3). See the file readme.

authority.quote: The party to whom the interrogatories are directed must serve the answers and any objections within 30 days after the service of the interrogatories, except that a defendant may serve answers or objections within 45 days after service of the process and initial pleading on that defendant. The court may allow a shorter or longer time.
authority.note: This row encodes the 30-day period measured from service of the interrogatories. The defendant's 45-day alternative runs from a DIFFERENT event -- service of process and the initial pleading -- and is a separate row (fl-rcp-1340a9-interrogatory-answers-defendant-45). The rule's closing sentence, 'The court may allow a shorter or longer time', means a scheduling order displaces this date; the engine cannot see one.

rules.label: Answers to interrogatories, defendant's alternative measured from service of process (Florida)

authority.quote: except that a defendant may serve answers or objections within 45 days after service of the process and initial pleading on that defendant
authority.note: A DIFFERENT CLOCK FROM A DIFFERENT EVENT, which is why it is its own row rather than a variant of the 30-day one. It is also an ALTERNATIVE the defendant MAY use, not a replacement -- 'a defendant may serve' -- so where both are available the defendant gets whichever is later, and choosing between them requires knowing both dates and that the party is a defendant. The engine has no party-role field and does not choose. No service extension is attached here: 2.514(b) adds time 'after service' of the thing that starts the clock, and this clock starts on service of process, not on service of a discovery request.

rules.label: Written response to a request to produce (Florida)

authority.quote: The party to whom the request is directed must serve a written response within 30 days after service of the request, except that a defendant may serve a response within 45 days after service of the process and initial pleading on that defendant. The court may allow a shorter or longer time.
authority.note: Unlike Illinois's Rule 214(a) and Ohio's Civ.R. 34(B), this is a real RESPONSE deadline, not a minimum period the requesting party must allow. Florida sets the response window directly, so the date this produces is a genuine due date rather than a floor. The defendant's 45-day alternative is a separate row for the same reason as the interrogatory one.

rules.label: Response to a request to produce, defendant's alternative measured from service of process (Florida)

authority.quote: except that a defendant may serve a response within 45 days after service of the process and initial pleading on that defendant
authority.note: Separate row for the same reason as the interrogatory 45-day alternative: a different clock from a different event, available to a defendant at the defendant's option. No service extension attached -- this clock starts on service of process, not on service of the request.

rules.label: Answer or objection to a request for admission before the matter is admitted (Florida)

authority.quote: The matter is admitted unless the party to whom the request is directed serves on the party requesting the admission a written answer or objection addressed to the matter within 30 days after service of the request or such shorter or longer time as the court may allow
authority.note: Like Illinois's Rule 216(c), missing this does not merely forfeit an objection -- it ADMITS the matter by operation of the rule, which makes it the most consequential deadline in the Florida civil set. The quoted text continues past what is reproduced here with further provisions on the form of an answer; only the timing sentence is encoded, and the 'shorter or longer time as the court may allow' clause means a court order displaces this date.

rules.label: Notice of appeal from a final order of a lower tribunal (Florida)

authority.quote: Jurisdiction of the court under this rule must be invoked by filing a notice with the clerk of the lower tribunal within 30 days of rendition of the order to be reviewed, except as provided in rule 9.140(c)(2).
authority.note: The trigger is RENDITION, which is a defined term of art in Florida appellate practice and is NOT the same as the date an order is signed or mailed. The engine takes the rendition date as given and does not compute it -- a user who supplies the signature date instead will get a wrong answer, and this note is the warning. No service extension: 2.514(b) extends periods measured 'after service', and this one is measured from rendition. NOT encoded: the 9.140(c)(2) criminal-appeal exception, and 9.110(c)'s separate administrative-appeal path which requires filing with two different clerks.
